newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds down but not out after strong Ifo, M3 data.
newsitem.headline: Bunds down but not out after strong Ifo, M3 data.

text.p: German Bunds weakened on Wednesday after the release of stronger-than-expected data for M3 money supply growth and the Ifo business climate index, but dealers said the market was not on the brink of a big sell-off.

The data dampened what little hope remained of another small cut in German interest rates and thereby hit shorter-dated maturities more than the long end of the market which was likely to consolidate, dealers and analysts said.
Nevertheless, 10-year Bunds staged a significant decline after the release of the Ifo west German business climate index.
The index jumped to 97.4 in October from 95.7 in September and was well above market expectations of 96.

But dealers said the fall in Bunds was a healthy move in a market that had been groping its way to contract high after contract high in recent weeks, climbing nearly one and a half points so far this month.

"The last bears had been slaughtered and bulls had had a free run. It's healthy if the market moves in the other direction from time to time," said Peter Kerger, a portfolio manager at Credit Suisse in Frankfurt.
The business expectations index for west Germany, regarded as a leading indicator, jumped two points to 103.1, showing that German firms were increasingly confident about their prospects.
Meanwhile, October M3 growth, the Bundesbank's main policy indicator, was unchanged from September at 8.4 percent.

Bunds showed little immediate reaction to the M3 news but slipped after the Ifo numbers released half an hour later, with the yield on the benchmark 10-year April 2006 Bund at 5.82 percent at 1030 GMT, up from 5.78 percent in early trade.

The December Bund future on the DTB German futures exchange, which has been rising steadily over the last month, reached a new contract high of 101.28 in early trade, fell as low as 100.91 after the numbers and was quoted at 100.95 at 1030 GMT.
The Bundesbank said M3 had been boosted by increased lending and by a sharp rise in sight deposits, probably due to money parked there to pay for Deutsche Telekom shares issued this week
"A rate cut is now virtually out of the question for most market participants," said Kerger at Credit Suisse.
Weak orders and output data for September had previously fuelled hopes of another Bundesbank credit easing, dealers said.
The long end of the market remained supported by the steepness of the German yield curve, with investors still attracted by relatively higher returns from longer-dated maturities, he added.
But, as rate hopes fade fast and yields at the short end of the market edge higher, the yield curve was set to flatten in the short term, Kerger said.

Bunds also remained underpinned by favourable conditions in the U.S. market, where Treasuries remained buoyed by fresh economic data suggesting the economy was slowing with no signs of inflation, dealers said.
Karen Kricks-Brunnlieb, head of bond analysis at Trinkaus & Burkhardt, predicted Bunds would consolidate for the time being and yields would rise gradually to six percent by the year-end.

"The data were clearly surprising," said Kricks-Brunnlieb. "But weak orders data recently tend to contradict the Ifo numbers. We will have to wait for fresh data on incoming orders to see whether the Ifo figures are confirmed."
In September, German industry orders fell 3.6 percent from August but economists expect them to be revised up. Industrial production fell 1.8 percent in September from August.
